newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: POLL-Ayala Land H1 seen flat, future bette.
newsitem.headline: POLL-Ayala Land H1 seen flat, future bette.

text.p: Ayala Land Inc's first-half performance will be uninspiring but it remains the top long-term pick among Philippine property stocks, analysts said on Tuesday.

A Reuters poll of seven stock brokerages showed that Ayala Land, the country's biggest property company, was expected to post an average 2.75 percent drop in profit for the the first half of 1997 to 2.47 billion pesos ($94 million), from 2.54 billion pesos a year ago.
But full-year 1997 could see renewed profit growth of 18 percent to 4.89 billion pesos, averages from the poll showed.

"Their first half will be flattish. It might be even less than that unless they do something unique like selling shares of a subsidiary or a plot of land," said one analyst who asked not to be named for fear of crossing one of the Philippines' most prestigious companies.
Ayala Land is part of Ayala Corp, the Philippines' oldest conglomerate, which traces its roots to 1834. Chairman Jaime Zobel de Ayala is the seventh-generation head of the family-controlled firm.

The firm's name is so prominent that the main street in Makati, the former wilderness area that Ayala converted into the country's premier business district, is called Ayala Avenue. This used to be the runway of a private Ayala airport and the control tower still stands there.
But analysts said the company's first-half performance reflected little of this corporate lustre.
"In the second quarter, there was a slowdown in take-up. Demand was affected by all the negative publicity of a property glut," said Noel Reyes, research head at Anscor Hagedorn Securities.
In May, Manila property stocks were battered after the market was gripped by rumours of an impending crash.
"I believe it is mostly perception. Once people realise their fears are unfounded, they will start buying," Reyes said.
Reyes added the prospects for lower interest rates in the second half of the year would also boost property demand.

Last month, the Philippine Central Bank raised its overnight lending rate to 20 percent from 13 percent to protect the peso from speculation as a result of the financial crisis in Thailand, which has seen speculative attacks on the Thai baht.
At present, the rate is at 15 percent but the central bank would like to lower it as soon as the Thai situation permits.
Bernadette Tamayo, analyst at BPI Capital Corp, said Ayala Land was a favourite stock because it had a wide range of products.
The over-supply in the property market was said to have been restricted to expensive office and residential premises and Ayala Land did not depend on those markets, she said.
Ayala Land is now developing an industrial park and company officials said its new investments would be in middle-income housing and infrastructure and developments outside Manila.
The rural market for property was seen as the brightest spot for the sector. "Provincial property plays -- screamingly cheap," brokerage Asia Equity said in its June report.
"One of them, Cebu Holdings Inc's operations were geared towards the fast-growing and dynamic Visayas and Mindanao areas," it said. Cebu Holdings is 47 percent owned by Ayala Land.
